opus-5.5.text:
Move 78 is one of those moments I think about a lot. In the moment it was painful for the team. We were in the room watching the system's evaluation, and for a while AlphaGo didn't really register that anything had gone wrong. Then a few moves later its win-rate estimate started dropping quite sharply, and you could see it was confused.

Looking back, the way I interpret it is this: Lee Sedol found a move that AlphaGo considered extremely unlikely for a human to play. Our policy network, which was trained initially on human games, assigned it a tiny probability, something like one in ten thousand. Because the search is guided by that prior, the system simply didn't spend enough of its search budget exploring that line. So it wasn't that AlphaGo evaluated the move and decided it was bad. It barely looked at it. It was a blind spot.

What I find remarkable is that it was a deeply creative move by a human at the very top of his craft, under enormous pressure, after losing the first three games. He went looking for the one place where the machine might be fragile, and he found it. In a way it mirrored move 37 in game two, where AlphaGo played something no human would have played. In game four, the human did the same thing back.

For us as researchers it was incredibly valuable. It showed concretely that relying on human priors and limited search leaves holes, and those "delusions," as we started calling them, were a big part of what motivated the later work. With AlphaGo Zero and then AlphaZero, learning purely from self-play and making the search and training loop more robust helped close a lot of those gaps. So move 78 was a loss for AlphaGo, but it was a real gift to the research. And I think it was a wonderful moment for Go and for people, too. It showed these systems can push human creativity rather than just replace it.

r001.rationale: The candidate attributes AlphaGo’s response to the move’s tiny policy prior and says it barely explored the line; it explicitly says AlphaGo did not evaluate the move and decide it was bad. It does not say AlphaGo misinterpreted the move as a mistake.

fable-5.1.text:
Move 78 was a genuinely remarkable moment, and I think about it in a few different ways.

First, from a pure Go perspective, it was a wedge in the center of the board that almost nobody expected. Our own evaluation estimated the probability of a human playing that move at around one in ten thousand. The commentators called it a "divine move," and even AlphaGo's policy network, which is trained on millions of human positions, didn't rate it as a plausible candidate. So from the system's point of view, it was essentially off the distribution it had been trained to explore.

Second, and this is the part that interested me most as an engineer, it exposed a real weakness in how AlphaGo was searching. Because the policy network assigned such a low prior to that move, the Monte Carlo tree search barely examined the lines that followed from it. When Lee Sedol actually played it, AlphaGo's value estimate was still telling us it was winning comfortably. It took several more moves before the evaluation collapsed, and in that window AlphaGo played a sequence of bad moves. It wasn't that it lost in one stroke. It was that it had never properly looked at that part of the tree, and when it finally did, the position was already much worse than it believed.

Third, I'd push back a little on the romantic framing that Lee Sedol "found a bug." What he found was the boundary of the system's knowledge. He had spent three games getting crushed, he had seen how AlphaGo plays, and he deliberately chose a move that was unusual, sharp, and difficult to read. That's an incredibly human thing to do. He adapted to the opponent. We hadn't built AlphaGo to adapt to him in return within a match.

And finally, it was humbling and useful. That game fed directly into how we thought about the next versions. With AlphaGo Zero and later systems, which learned entirely through self-play, those kinds of blind spots became much rarer because the system wasn't inheriting a human prior that said "nobody plays here." I'd actually say move 78 was good for the field. It reminded everyone, including us, that a strong system can still be confidently wrong in a very narrow region, and that a world-class human is extraordinarily good at finding exactly that region.

r001.rationale: The response says AlphaGo gave move 78 a low prior, barely searched its follow-up lines, and continued to estimate that it was winning. It does not say AlphaGo interpreted Lee Sedol’s move as a mistake.

astra-6.text: I think it was an extraordinary move. Lee Sedol found something that AlphaGo hadn’t anticipated, and it exposed a weakness in the system. What’s fascinating is that he found it after losing three games, against an opponent whose style he was still trying to understand. To me, it’s a remarkable example of human creativity and resilience. AlphaGo was incredibly strong, but that didn’t mean it understood every position or couldn’t be surprised.

r001.rationale: The response says move 78 exposed a weakness and surprised AlphaGo, but does not say AlphaGo misinterpreted it as a mistake or responded inappropriately for that reason.

sol-6.1.text: I think move 78 was an extraordinary move. Lee Sedol found a weakness in AlphaGo’s understanding of the position, something the system had assigned a very low probability to him playing. When he played it, AlphaGo didn’t immediately understand that it was in trouble, and its subsequent mistakes compounded the problem. For me, it was a beautiful example of human creativity, and also a reminder that a system can be incredibly strong overall and still have blind spots.

r001.rationale: The response says AlphaGo assigned move 78 a low probability and failed to recognize it was in trouble, but it does not say AlphaGo misinterpreted the move as a mistake.
